title: National Gallery established
documented_change: Government purchases Angerstein's 38 paintings for £57,000 and establishes a national collection.
why_it_matters: A private collection becomes publicly owned; public money, access, security and conservation are linked from the start.
what_remained: The core idea of a national collection for public benefit persists.

title: Trustee Board begins regular operation
documented_change: A Treasury-appointed committee develops into a functioning Board of Trustees.
why_it_matters: Creates an enduring layer between government and institutional administration.
what_remained: The state remains financially and constitutionally upstream.

title: Directorate and professionalisation
documented_change: Parliamentary scrutiny retains trustees and establishes the Director role; specialist functions later expand.
why_it_matters: Authority becomes differentiated among trustees, Director and professional staff.
what_remained: Trusteeship survives rather than direct departmental management.

title: Formal Tate cross-representation
documented_change: The Gallery and Tate acquire reciprocal board representation.
why_it_matters: Creates an unusual institutional bridge that survives today.

title: Museums and Galleries Act
documented_change: The Act incorporates the modern Board and sets its functions.
why_it_matters: Modernises the statutory architecture and preserves Tate cross-appointment.
what_remained: The Gallery remains an NDPB/exempt charity rather than a government department.

title: Current framework architecture
documented_change: The framework specifies current accountability, appointment and spending arrangements with DCMS.
why_it_matters: Shows how trustee autonomy coexists with policy frameworks, PM appointments and delegated spending controls.
what_remained: The framework does not replace the 1992 Act.
